chunks: Buck performance over PVT. The question: How does buck performance vary with process, voltage, and temperature (PVT)?
PVT stands for process, voltage, and temperature. The same buck converter behaves differently from one unit to the next, across its input and load range, and from cold to hot.
This page is about finding the worst case in each of these and making sure the design still works there. You design with margins, then check the corners on the bench.
Imagine a bridge that must stay safe in summer heat, winter cold, and rush-hour traffic, and also if the steel is a bit weaker than the spec.
You do not check only the average case. You check the worst combinations.
The bridge picture does not show that for a converter, the worst case differs by quantity: ripple is worst at high input, and heat is worst at high input, full load, and hot.
Ripple rises with V IN and, at 18 volts, tolerance spread alone moves it between 0. 60 amps and 1. 10 amps (best to worst).
Designing at nominal L and f SW would under-estimate peak current and saturation stress by about 0. 15 amps on the peak.
Process: unit-to-unit variation in parts, such as ±1% on a reference or ±20% on an inductor. Voltage: the range of input voltage and load that the converter sees.
Temperature: the operating range, which changes resistance and ratings. Corner: an extreme combination of these.
Tolerance stack-up: adding up the worst-case errors from several parts.
Take an inductor whose copper wire has a resistance (DCR) of 50 milliohms at 25 degrees Celsius. Copper resistance rises about 0.
39% per °C, so at 105 degrees Celsius it rises by 80 times 0. 39 % about 31 % , to about 66 milliohms. At 3 amps, the loss goes from 3 squared times 0. 05 equals 0.
45 watts to about 0. 59 watts. So the hot corner has more loss, which makes it even hotter. That is the whole idea.
"Process is part-to-part spread: reference, oscillator, current limit, FET resistance, and L and C tolerance.
Voltage is input range, output and load: at high input, duty is smallest, ripple and switching loss are highest and on-time is shortest.
Temperature raises DCR and R DS(on) so efficiency falls when hot, ferrite saturates earlier, ceramic capacitance and electrolytic ESR shift.
I'd find the worst corner for each metric, stack up tolerances for accuracy, and verify and margin across corners."
